brief.topic: When Waiting Longer Does Not Bring Success Closer

s01: Five failures have passed. Is success now closer?
Suppose every attempt succeeds with chance one quarter, independently of the others.
One more failure has chance three quarters.
Two more failures have chance nine sixteenths. This does not change after five failures.
Let T be the attempt of the first success.
The chance T exceeds n is three quarters to the power n.
Given five failures, the chance of two more is the chance of seven divided by the chance of five.
The first five factors cancel, leaving three quarters squared. This is the memoryless property.
It describes this fixed probability model, not every kind of waiting.
Now draw from a bag with one success token and three failures, without replacement.
After two failures, two tokens remain. The next chance of success is one half, not one quarter.
Removing failures changes the state. A model has no memory only when its assumptions make the past irrelevant to what remains.
